events.text: The Mannheim Observatory was a tower observatory built between 1772 and 1774 in Mannheim , Germany
The Mannheim Observatory remained in operation until 1880
The observatory was transferred to Karlsruhe and finally in 1898 , was established on the Königstuhl near Heidelberg
The observatory tower was restored in 1905–1906
The tower houses studio flats since 1958
The Physics Institute was established in 1751 in Heidelberg.
In 1759, Mayer observed the return of the comet predicted by Edmond Halley.
Mayer observed the Transit of Venus across the Sun on 6 June 1761 from a temporary Observatory built of wood by Karl Theodor in the Orangery in the park of Schwetzingen Castle.
The observations convinced the elector as early as July to begin work on an observatory building on the palace roof, which was inaugurated in 1764.
Mayer observed another Transit of Venus on 3 June 1769.
On New Years Day 1771 Mayer finally presented a memorandum on the construction of an observatory to the Mannheim Court.
In 1772 the Elector charged the Court Chamberlain with the construction of the observatory.
In the same year the foundation stone of the tower next to Schloss Mannheim, in the vicinity of the Jesuit College was laid.
Elector Karl Theodor left the Palatinate in 1778, to govern Bavaria.
The ex-Jesuit John Fischer resigned in 1788 after only a year and a half.
Peter Ungeschick died in 1790 on the return journey from studying in Paris.
Roger Barry fell ill in 1810
Roger Barry died in 1813
Heinrich Christian Schumacher was Director from 1813 to 1815
Bernhard Nicolai was Court Astronomer from 1816
Bernhard Nicolai died in 1846
It was decided to end the Institute by appointing no new Court Astronomer on 10 June 1850
The Heidelberg professor Nell took over the unpaid supervision of the institute in 1852
This modest institute planned renewal with the purchase of a six-stage telescope in 1859
Eduard Schönfeld was appointed Director with a salary in 1859.
The Astronomische Gesellschaft was founded on 28 August 1863 in Heidelberg.
Schönfeld left for Bonn in 1875.
Karl Wilhelm Valentiner took over the Mannheim Directorship in 1875.
The Observatory was moved to a makeshift building in Karlsruhe in 1880.
Max Wolf had already built a private observatory in his parents house in 1880.
A deputation of Heidelberg professors petitioned the Grand Duke of Karlsruhe for a University research and teaching observatory in 1892.
The Großherzogliche Bergsternwarte at Königstuhl was ceremonially inaugurated by Frederick I , Grand Duke of Baden on 20 June 1898.
After Valentiners retirement in 1909 , both departments were amalgamated.
In 1983 the Mannheim instruments were donated to the State Museum of Technology and Industry in Mannheim
The 1859 six-stage telescope was given to the city of Karlsruhe in 1957 for the establishment of the Public Astronomical Observatory of Karlsruhe
